opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the way to understand it is that each model is almost its own company. Let's say in some year you train a model that costs $100 million. You deploy it, and over its lifetime it brings in, say, $200 million of revenue. The inference costs of serving it are real, but the gross margins are healthy, so that model, considered on its own, is a profitable business. It paid back its training cost and then some.

But in the same year that model is earning money, you're training the next one, and that one costs a billion dollars. The year after, it earns two or three billion, and meanwhile you're spending ten billion on the one after that. So if you look at the company's income statement in any given year, you see a big loss, because you're comparing this year's revenue from the last model against this year's spending on the next, much bigger one. The losses come from the exponential scaling of investment, not from the unit economics being bad.

So the accounting picture and the economic picture diverge. If you did the accounting cohort by cohort, model by model, each one looks like a decent investment. The company as a whole looks like it's losing money because every year you're making a bet that's ten times bigger than the last.

The real question, and it's the one I think people should actually focus on, is whether that continues. Two things can happen. One, the scaling keeps paying off: each model is good enough to justify the next round of investment, and at some point the curve flattens, either because you run into physical limits like compute, power and chips, or because the models are just good enough. Then you stop growing training spend tenfold a year and the profits from the deployed models show up on the income statement. Two, at some point a model doesn't earn back what it cost. You spent ten billion and it brought in five, and then you have a real problem.

So I don't think "AI companies lose money" by itself tells you much. What matters is whether each generation earns back its cost with margin, and how disciplined you are about not overbuilding relative to the revenue you can actually see coming. That last part is something we think about a lot, because if you get the timing wrong on compute, being a year early on a huge commitment can be really dangerous even if you're right about where things end up.

r001.rationale: The response explains that company losses arise because spending on each successor model grows sharply while revenue comes from previously deployed models, even when each model is profitable on its own.

r002.rationale: It says the scaling may flatten, after which training spend stops growing tenfold each year and profits from deployed models appear on the income statement.

fable-5.1.text:
So the way I think about it is that you have to separate the economics of a single model from the economics of the company, because they look completely different.

Take any given model. You spend, let's say, a hundred million dollars to train it. Then you deploy it, and over its lifetime it brings in, say, two hundred million in revenue. The inference costs are real but they're a fraction of that revenue. So that model, considered on its own, is a profitable business. Positive gross margin, and actually positive return on the training capital too.

The problem is that while that model is out in the world making money, you're training the next one. And the next one costs a billion dollars, not a hundred million. So in the year that the hundred-million-dollar model is earning its two hundred million, the company's P&L shows a billion in training spend against two hundred million in revenue. It looks like you're hemorrhaging money. Then next year the billion-dollar model earns two billion, but now you're spending ten billion on the one after that. Every year the company loses more in absolute terms, and every individual model is a good investment.

It's basically the dynamic of a company that's reinvesting in its own growth at an exponential rate. If you froze the frontier tomorrow and said no more scaling, these companies would become very profitable very quickly. The losses are a choice to keep scaling, not evidence that the underlying product doesn't work.

Now, the honest caveat is that this story depends on the pattern continuing. It depends on each ten-x increase in training cost producing a model that captures roughly ten-x more value. So far that has held, and I'd argue it's held better than most people expected. But it's a bet. If at some point the next generation doesn't generate the revenue to justify it, then you don't get that terminal profitable state, you just get a very expensive model and a hole in the ground. I think that's unlikely, but that's the actual risk, and it's a different risk than "the margins are bad."

r001.rationale: It explains that each model can be profitable while escalating training costs for successor models make the company’s overall spending exceed revenue.

r002.rationale: It describes profitability if scaling stops, but does not situate a “country of geniuses in a data center” equilibrium in a regime where training scale-up has leveled off.

astra-6.text:
Well, positive gross margins mean that serving the models brings in more revenue than it costs to serve them. That doesn’t mean the company as a whole is profitable, because you’re also spending money training the next generation of models, doing research, and building the infrastructure for future growth.

So you have to separate two questions. One is: is there a business in selling the models you’ve already built? The other is: how much are you investing in what comes next? You can have a healthy business on the first dimension and still lose a lot of money overall because the second is so expensive.

Of course, calling something an investment doesn’t automatically make it a good investment. Eventually, the revenue those investments generate has to justify their cost. The real question is whether future demand and future model capabilities will support the spending you’re doing today.

r001.rationale: The response says losses can result from spending on training next-generation models, research, and infrastructure, but does not say training spend is increasing exponentially.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention the “country of geniuses in a data center,” an economic equilibrium, or training scale-up becoming more level.

sol-6.1.text:
The key distinction is between the cost of serving a model and the cost of developing the next one. Positive gross margins mean that when someone pays to use a model, the revenue exceeds the compute cost of answering their requests. But that doesn’t cover the training runs, the research staff, and all the experiments that went into building it.

And you’re paying for the next generation before you earn revenue from it. So you can have a business where every additional customer contributes money, but the company as a whole is losing money because it’s investing heavily in future models.

That can make sense if revenue keeps growing fast enough. But positive gross margins alone don’t establish that those investments will pay off. You still have to ask whether the future revenue will justify the development costs.

r001.rationale: The response links company losses to investment in future models, but does not say that spending on successor training is increasing exponentially.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention a “country of geniuses in a data center” or an equilibrium where model-training scale-up has leveled off.
